subject: opportunity-cost
title: Opportunity Cost: The Hidden Price of Yes
summary: Every yes spends scarce time or money—so the real cost is the next-best path you shut down.

keys.answer: The value of the next-best alternative you give up when you make a decision—not every other option, and not only the sticker price.

keys.prompt: Why does scarcity force opportunity costs?
keys.answer: Unlimited wants chase limited time, money, and resources, so every choice trades one path for another.

keys.prompt: Why is the true cost of college more than tuition?
keys.answer: You also give up the wages you could have earned by working instead—an implicit opportunity cost on top of explicit tuition.

cards.title: A $7 smoothie
cards.text: At the mall, a smoothie costs $7. Most people ask only "Do I want it?" Put on economist glasses: what else could that $7—or that ten minutes—have become?

cards.question: College tuition is $10,000 a year. You could earn $20,000 working instead. About what do economists say the true yearly cost of attending is?
cards.reveal: Explicit tuition ($10,000) plus the implicit opportunity cost of not working ($20,000) makes about $30,000 a year—before counting later higher earnings that can reverse the math.

cards.title: Scarcity → choice → cost
cards.text: Scarcity means wants outrun the time, money, and resources available. That forces choices. Every choice has an opportunity cost: the value of the next-best alternative you give up.
cards.example: Federal Reserve education materials stress the chain: scarcity, then choice, then opportunity cost as the foundation of economic thinking.

cards.title: Next-best, not every-best
cards.text: Opportunity cost is only the option you would have picked next—not the sum of every rejected idea. You can only spend the same hour once.
cards.example: Say… after school you could practice golf, code an app, or watch a show. If golf wins, the opportunity cost is whichever of coding or the show you valued second—not both stacked.

why.q: Why isn't the cost "everything else I might have done"?
why.a: Those alternatives compete for the same scarce slot. You forgo the single next-best use, not every use at once.

examples_by_interest.golf: Say… you take a paid lesson instead of a free range hour with friends. The opportunity cost is that friend session—the next-best use of the afternoon.
examples_by_interest.soccer: Say… you pick an extra practice over a weekend job shift. The opportunity cost is the pay (and experience) from that shift.
examples_by_interest.business: Say… you spend Saturday restocking your stand instead of testing a new product. The opportunity cost is the learning from that test.

cards.title: Explicit vs implicit
cards.text: Explicit costs are the obvious dollars out the door—tuition, gear, rent. Implicit costs are what you give up without a receipt, like wages you never earned while in class.
cards.example: Economists add both. A year of college can cost tuition plus the paycheck you skipped by not working full-time.

cards.title: People forget the trade
cards.text: Opportunity costs are easy to neglect. A St. Louis Fed essay suggests seeing a $7 smoothie as a movie ticket or $7 for a future goal—not just a drink.
cards.example: When the next-best use is named out loud, people buy less often. Spelling the trade changes the decision.

cards.question: Name one "yes" you are considering (a purchase, a team, a project). What is the single next-best use of that time or money—and would you still say yes?
nudges: Write the next-best option in one sentence before deciding.
Would your answer change if the cost were tomorrow's self, not today's?

questions.q: Opportunity cost is best defined as:

options.text: The value of the next-best alternative given up
options.why: Yes—that is the Fed and textbook definition.

options.text: Only the sticker price you pay
options.why: Sticker price is explicit; opportunity cost includes the alternative forgone.

options.text: The sum of every option you imagined
A fee banks charge for saving
options.why: Opportunity cost is a decision concept, not a bank fee.

questions.q: Why can college cost more than tuition alone?

options.text: You also give up wages you could have earned
options.why: Forgone earnings are a classic implicit opportunity cost.
Books can add explicit costs; the key idea here is forgone pay.

options.text: Opportunity cost never applies to school
options.why: Time in school is a major opportunity-cost case.
Choices still trade off scarce years.

questions.q: You have one Saturday. You pick building a product over a paid shift. The opportunity cost is mainly:

options.text: The pay (and experience) from that shift
options.why: That was the next-best use of the day.

options.text: Every job you might ever have
options.why: Only the next-best alternative for that Saturday.
Time is scarce even when money isn't spent.

options.text: Only the snacks you bought while building
options.why: Snacks are a small explicit cost; the big trade is the shift.

cards.prompt: Explain this to someone at dinner in 3 sentences.
starters: College (or any big yes) also costs…

video.title: Opportunity Cost: The Hidden Cost of Everything
video.why: Adds forgone wages to tuition so you see why economists count implicit costs—not only the bill you pay.
